thread.title: NRC Group Warrants: Too Cheap By A Wide Margin - NRCG Wt 06.24 (NYSEMKT:NRCG.WS)

author: Dane Capital Management, LLC
title: NRC Group Warrants: Too Cheap By A Wide Margin - NRCG Wt 06.24 (NYSEMKT:NRCG.WS)
text:
On Friday after the close, Waitr ( WTRH ) announced a tender to its warrant holders that they could exchange their warrants ( OTC:WTRHW ) (half-warrants) for .18 shares of Waitr stock. With warrants trading at $1.61 per half-warrant, and shares at $12.30, this represented value of $2.214 per share, or a healthy 38% premium. On a full warrant basis, that represents approximately $4.43 per share. With that as back-drop, we thought we'd revisit NRC Group's warrants ( NRCG.WS ) which we believe are profoundly undervalued based on the price of underlying NRC Group ( NRCG ) shares. To be clear, as we will show below, our view on NRC warrants is not predicated on NRC Group shares being undervalued, but is based on data that demonstrates their significant mispricing.
We have written extensively on NRC Group ( NRCG ), which we believe is materially undervalued. Our original write-up can be found here and a more recent write-up including a presentation can be found here . NRC Group competes in the environmental and waste services space, has high customer retention and recurring revenue on non-discretionary spend items, a diversified customer base (5000+ customers), deep competitive moats due to regulatory challenges for new players, and low cap-ex. At a comparable multiple to peers, shares would trade at $18, or 90% upside. Notably, this includes the dilutive impact of outstanding warrants.
According to our analysis, at the NRCG's current price of $9.46, NRC Group warrants ( NRCG.WS ) should be trading around $2.00 or more than 100% above their current price of $0.90. We believe that if NRCG shares merely remain at current levels, as SPAC arbs sell their remaining warrant holdings - we believe their ongoing unwanted warrant "inventory" is the primary reason for the mispricing - the warrants will converge upon fair value. Additionally, NRC Group management could offer a warrant exchange at a hefty premium to current prices, thereby eliminating potential future dilution, at what we believe will prove bargain basement prices. We wrote about the concept of SPAC arbs holding unwanted warrants in a write-up on Hostess Brands ( TWNK ) in August 2016. The thesis that warrants were undervalued and would converge on fair value and that the stock would appreciate played out then and we think this will prove to be a sequel.

A fair question is how we arrive at a price of $2.00 (or more) as a fair value for NRCG.WS at the current underlying price of NRCG. We employ 2 methodologies and have an additional source as a sanity check.
First, we employ a modified Black-Scholes formula that accounts for the NRC Group's ability to force conversion at $18 per share if the warrants trade above $18 for a period of 20 days in a 30 day trading period. A useful model can be found here . In this model you can plug in the cap (forced conversion price), current share price, strike price, expected volatility, risk-free rate, dividend yield (none in this case), and duration (expected life). Below we post results from a 30% and 40% implied volatility. Of course you can use your own.
Source: Capped Option Valuation Models
Source: Capped Option Valuation Models
One may argue that 30% is too high an implied volatility. Given the historic trading of other post-merger SPAC warrants and from additional information provided below, we believe our volatility assumptions accurately reflect reality.
Second, we look at where former SPAC warrants historically trade and also assess the premiums they receive in the case of a warrant tender. A potential positive outcome is that for NRC Group warrant holders is that they will be exchanged for cash or stock at a premium to current prices. Unless NRC Group announces a huge premium, we hope that they don't offer warrant tender in the near-term because we believe the stock and warrants are both materially undervalued, and we'd like them both to appreciate first. We have spoken to NRC Group management regarding cleaning up the capital structure by eliminating warrants and our impression is that is in their medium-term plans (within a couple quarters).
For those curious about the history of warrant tenders, we have listed multiple below. Tenders have been announced on out of the money warrants as well as in the money warrants. In fact, ConvergeOne ( CVON ) announced its first tender when its shares were at $7.92 (it re-upped its tender from $0.90 to $1.20 per warrant when the stock traded up to $8.62). At a stock price more than $0.80 below that of NRC Group, warrant holders were offered $0.30 more per warrant than NRCG.WS closed today.
In general, shares of the underlying security perform well from the period of announcement to the tender's expiration. Willscot ( WSC ) is an exception, although we'd attribute that to a brutal 4Q 2018 for leveraged equities - particularly those with a SPAC heritage (see write-up on this topic here ).
This chart above illustrates that other than ConvergeOne and Hennessy, which became Bluebird ( BLBD ), all warrant offers have been in excess of $2, even that of FG Holdings ( FG ), at $2.16, which was a sub-$9 stock at the time of the warrant exchange tender. Playa ( PLYA ) was $10.25 when they tendered, a mere $0.80 higher than NRC Group currently trades, and on a whole warrant basis the offer was $3.09, more than 3-times NRC warrants' current price (the offer was .1 shares per 1/3 warrant). Relative to the prices in the chart above, NRCG.WS looks like a significant outlier based on the price of underlying NRCG shares.
We have spoken with many managements regarding their rationale for cleaning up outstanding warrants. Their reasons are two-fold: first, and most importantly, they are bullish regarding the prospects of their business and would like to minimize dilution by doing so while their stock price is still low. Clearly, this was done to great effect by Bluebird, which got a bargain, in part, because the exchange was done at the time of the merger close. With Bluebird shares now at ~$20 they saved themselves from significant dilution by eliminating warrants early and inexpensively (notably, NRC Group's SPAC sponsor Hennessy, is the same sponsor as for Bluebird). Similarly, ConvergeOne took its warrants out cheaply, setting themselves up for an acquisition at a solid premium. We believe Waitr has strong fundamentals and will similarly exhibit solid results and share appreciation. Second, the elimination of warrants cleans up the capital structure and makes the stock more attractive and investible to potential shareholders.
We have been surprised by the number of institutional investors who have told us (a point echoed to us by several sell-side analysts who cover former SPACs) that they won't invest in companies with outstanding warrants. We see little difference between warrants and stock options which are given out like candy on halloween by Amazon ( AMZN ), Apple ( AAPL ), Facebook ( FB ), etc. We recognize that many investors include options as a real cost, and they factor them into their analyses. We're unaware of investors that won't invest in companies that grant options (or they'd probably have nothing to invest in). However, there are investors that religiously avoid companies with warrants, regardless of valuation.
A final sanity check we employ is the TPG algorithm. Specifically, in TPG's current SPAC ( TPGH ) their prospectus provides a warrant exchange algorithm which illustrates the share exchange ratio they intend to offer for warrants at various times remaining until expiration and at various stock prices. Source: TPG Holdings Prospectus page 126
While the above only begins at $10 per share, we can iterate that at $9.46 and 57 months remaining until warrant expiration, the exchange offer would be approximately .244 shares per warrant (notably TPGH and NRCG both trade full warrants with $18 take-outs). This equates to a value of $2.31 per NRCG warrant. We are not suggesting that they trade there, because warrants tend to be exchanged at a premium to their then trading price. However, it certainly seems reasonable that they should trade at $1.80 (100% upside to current), and with a ~30% take-out premium, be exchanged for a value of $2.31.
To reiterate TPG's warrant exchange formula is from its initial prospectus. They do not know which business they will buy. They do not know the implied volatility of the underlying security that will one day exist. By virtue of putting this in their prospectus, they are indicating that they see clear value in eliminating warrants, and they are assuming a healthy implied volatility. Certainly, this is strong validation of our valuation based on Black-Scholes and on comparative warrant valuations.
One can argue whether NRCG warrants should trade at $1.50 or $1.70 or $2.20, but the data clearly supports this view and out opinion that $0.90 is disconnected from any justifiable valuation methodology.
Conclusion
We believe shares of NRCG are materially undervalued, and have a price that is disconnected from company fundamentals. We think this is a reflection of sloppy trading as a recent merged SPAC, lack of institutional awareness, and a small float. Notably this resembles Bluebird's initial trading - which turned into a big winner. With a higher growth rate than peers and an exceptional free cash flow story, we are confident shares will eventually garner a premium multiple. We believe that NRCG warrants are especially interesting as they are significantly mispriced based on the current equity value of NRCG. If NRCG appreciates and its warrants converge on fair value, the warrants should produce a multi-bagger return. Finally, we note that the warrants are quite liquid and we believe there is also significant availability from SPAC arbs.
